tredive.explanation: "Tredive" means "thirty". To say 31, put the one first: "enogtredive" (thirty-one), literally "one-and-thirty".

tredje.explanation: "Tredje" means "third". To give a date, say: "den tredje oktober" (the third of October).

tres.explanation: "Tres" means "sixty". Do not mix it up with "tre" (three): "tre børn" means three children, and "tres børn" means sixty children.

tretten.explanation: "Tretten" means "thirteen". To say how many things there are, put it before the noun: "tretten æg" (thirteen eggs).

trist.explanation: "Trist" means "sad". Besides a person who feels sad, it also describes a gloomy thing. To describe gray weather, say: "Vejret er trist i dag" (The weather is gloomy today).

trivsel.explanation: "Trivsel" means "well-being". It comes from the verb "at trives" (to thrive). To say you feel at home somewhere, use the verb: "Jeg trives her" (I feel at home here).

tro.explanation: "Tro" means "faith". To say someone keeps their faith, say: "Hun mister aldrig sin tro" (She never loses her faith). To say you think something is true, use the verb "at tro" (to believe): "Jeg tror, det er rigtigt" (I think it is right).

trods.explanation: "Trods" means "despite". To say what you went on despite, name the obstacle right after it: "trods regnen" (despite the rain).

trods alt.explanation: "Trods alt" means "after all". It is built from "trods" (despite) and "alt" (everything), so it is literally "despite everything". To say the evening was good in the end: "Var festen god?" "Ja, det var trods alt en god aften." (Was the party good? Yes, it was a good evening after all.)

troende.explanation: "Troende" means "believing". It comes from the verb "at tro" (to believe). To describe a person who has a faith, say: "en troende muslim" (a believing Muslim). With "de" (the), it names the people: "de troende" (the believers).

trofast.explanation: "Trofast" means "faithful". It is built from "tro" (loyal) and "fast" (firm). To say a partner cheated, use the opposite, "utro" (unfaithful): "Han var utro" (He was unfaithful).

troskab.explanation: "Troskab" means "loyalty". It is built from "tro" (faithful) and "-skab", an ending that makes a noun, as in "venskab" (friendship). To name the opposite, say: "Utroskab ødelagde ægteskabet" (Infidelity ruined the marriage).

trusser.explanation: "Trusser" means "panties". It is plural, like "panties" in English. For men's underwear, say "underbukser" (underpants): "Jeg har købt nye underbukser" (I bought new underpants).

tryg.explanation: "Tryg" means "safe", as in feeling looked after. To say children feel safe with someone: "Børnene er trygge hos deres bedstemor" (The children feel safe with their grandmother). To say you feel uneasy, use the opposite, "utryg" (uneasy): "Han er utryg ved at flyve" (He is uneasy about flying).

tryghed.explanation: "Tryghed" means "security". It is built from the adjective "tryg" (safe) and the ending "-hed". To say something gives security, use it with "at give" (to give): "Rutiner giver børn tryghed" (Routines give children security).

trygt.explanation: "Trygt" means "safely". It comes from the adjective "tryg" (safe). To tell someone they need not worry about doing something, say: "Du kan trygt spørge" (You can safely ask).

trådløs.explanation: "Trådløs" means "wireless". It is built from "tråd" (wire) and "-løs" (-less).

træg.explanation: "Træg" means "sluggish". To say you have little energy, say: "Jeg føler mig træg i dag" (I feel sluggish today).

træning.explanation: "Træning" means "training session". It comes from the verb "at træne" (to train). To say you have practice, use it with "at have" (to have): "Jeg har træning i aften" (I have training tonight).

træningstøj.explanation: "Træningstøj" means "workout clothes". It is built from "træning" (training) and "tøj" (clothes). To remind someone to pack it for the gym: "Husk dit træningstøj" (Remember your workout clothes).

træt.explanation: "Træt" means "tired". To say you are fed up with something, add "af" (of): "Jeg er træt af støjen" (I am fed up with the noise).

træt af.explanation: "Træt af" means "tired of". To say you have had enough of something: "Jeg er træt af støjen" (I am tired of the noise). Without "af", it is about needing sleep: "Jeg er træt" (I am tired).

træthed.explanation: "Træthed" means "tiredness". It is built from the adjective "træt" (tired) and the ending "-hed". To say you are struggling with it: "Jeg kæmper med træthed" (I am struggling with tiredness).

trøst.explanation: "Trøst" means "comfort", as in consolation for someone who is sad. To say something helps only a little, say: "Det er en lille trøst" (That is a small comfort).

tun.explanation: "Tun" means "tuna". It joins other words, as in "tunsalat" (tuna salad): "Jeg tager en sandwich med tunsalat" (I will take a sandwich with tuna salad).

tung.explanation: "Tung" means "heavy". To say food feels heavy in the stomach, say: "tung mad" (heavy food).

turkis.explanation: "Turkis" means "turquoise". English speakers should spell it with a "k" where English has "qu".

tusind.explanation: "Tusind" means "thousand". To say a year, count in hundreds instead: 1999 is "nitten hundrede og nioghalvfems" (nineteen hundred and ninety-nine).

tusind tak.explanation: "Tusind tak" means "thanks a lot", literally "a thousand thanks". To thank a host after a meal, add "for" and what you thank for: "Tusind tak for maden" (Thanks a lot for the meal).

tusindvis.explanation: "Tusindvis" means "thousands". To say what is counted, add "af" (of) and the noun: "tusindvis af mennesker" (thousands of people).

tvetydig.explanation: "Tvetydig" means "ambiguous". The start "tve-" means "two", as in "tvilling" (twin).

tvivlsom.explanation: "Tvivlsom" means "doubtful". It is built from "tvivl" (doubt) and the ending "-som". To say a person feels unsure, use "usikker" (unsure): "Jeg er usikker" (I am unsure).

tvungen.explanation: "Tvungen" means "forced". It comes from the verb "at tvinge" (to force). To say who is forced to do what, use "til at" (into): "De tvinger ham til at flytte" (They are forcing him to move).

tværtimod.explanation: "Tværtimod" means "on the contrary". To answer a question by saying the opposite is true: "Generer jeg dig?" "Tværtimod!" (Am I bothering you? On the contrary!)

tydelig.explanation: "Tydelig" means "clear", as in easy to see or understand. To ask someone to speak so you can understand, say: "Tal tydeligt" (Speak clearly). For clear water or clear skies, use "klar" (clear): "klart vand" (clear water).

tydeligvis.explanation: "Tydeligvis" means "obviously". It is built from "tydelig" (clear) and "-vis", an ending like English "-ly". To say the signs show nobody is home: "Der er tydeligvis ingen hjemme" (Obviously nobody is home).

tyggegummi.explanation: "Tyggegummi" means "chewing gum". It is built from "at tygge" (to chew) and "gummi" (rubber). The part "gummi" also appears in "gummistøvler" (rubber boots).

tyk.explanation: "Tyk" means "thick". To say a jacket is thick: "Jakken er tyk" (The jacket is thick). About a person it means "fat" and is as blunt as that English word.

tynd.explanation: "Tynd" means "thin". It also describes watery liquids: "tynd suppe" (thin soup). To describe a person as slim, say "slank" (slim): "Hun er slank" (She is slim).

tyngdekraft.explanation: "Tyngdekraft" means "gravity". It is built from "tyngde" (weight) and "kraft" (force), so it is literally "weight force". To say why things fall: "Tyngdekraften trækker tingene ned" (Gravity pulls things down).

typisk.explanation: "Typisk" means "typical". To complain that something bad happened again, say just: "Typisk!" (Typical!)

tyrkiet.explanation: "Tyrkiet" means "Turkey", as in the country. To say the bird, use "en kalkun" (a turkey): "Jeg har en kalkun i ovnen" (I have a turkey in the oven).

tyrkisk.explanation: "Tyrkisk" means "Turkish". To ask whether someone knows the language: "Kan du tyrkisk?" (Do you know Turkish?)

tysk.explanation: "Tysk" means "German". To name the school subject: "Vi har tysk i dag" (We have German today).

tyskland.explanation: "Tyskland" means "Germany". It is built from "tysk" (German) and "land" (country). Germany is the only country that shares a land border with Denmark.

tyve.explanation: "Tyve" means "twenty". To say 22, put the two first: "toogtyve" (twenty-two), literally "two-and-twenty".

tyvende.explanation: "Tyvende" means "twentieth". To name the 1900s, say: "det tyvende århundrede" (the twentieth century).

tåbelig.explanation: "Tåbelig" means "foolish". To say "stupid" in everyday speech, use "dum": "Det var en dum idé" (That was a stupid idea).

tåge.explanation: "Tåge" means "fog". To say the weather is foggy, use the adjective "tåget" (foggy): "Det er tåget i dag" (It is foggy today).

tålmodig.explanation: "Tålmodig" means "patient". The opposite is "utålmodig" (impatient): "Børnene er utålmodige" (The children are impatient).

related.en: to bear, to put up with

tålmodighed.explanation: "Tålmodighed" means "patience". It is built from the adjective "tålmodig" (patient) and the ending "-hed". To tell someone to be patient: "Vær tålmodig" (Be patient).

tæt.explanation: "Tæt" means "dense". To describe thick fog: "Der er tæt tåge" (There is dense fog). To say a place is close, use "tæt på" (close to): "Jeg bor tæt på skolen" (I live close to the school).

tæt på.explanation: "Tæt på" means "close to". To say you nearly did something: "Han var tæt på at vinde" (He came close to winning). To say a place is far away, use "langt fra" (far from): "Skolen ligger langt fra stationen" (The school is far from the station).

tøj.explanation: "Tøj" means "clothes". This word has no article, so leave out "et": say "mit tøj" (my clothes) or "noget tøj" (some clothes). To point to one piece of clothing, use its name: "en trøje" (a sweater).

tømmer.explanation: "Tømmer" means "timber". Do not mix it up with "tømmer" from "at tømme" (to empty): "Jeg tømmer skabet" (I empty the cabinet).

tømmermænd.explanation: "Tømmermænd" means "a hangover". The word is always plural. To say you have one: "Jeg har tømmermænd" (I have a hangover).

tør.explanation: "Tør" means "dry". It is also a form of the verb "at turde" (to dare): "Jeg tør ikke" (I dare not).

tørret frugt.explanation: "Tørret frugt" means "dried fruit". "Tørret" (dried) comes from the verb "at tørre" (to dry). To say what you add to your porridge: "Jeg putter tørret frugt i havregrøden" (I put dried fruit in the porridge).

tørstig.explanation: "Tørstig" means "thirsty". The noun is "tørst" (thirst). To say you are thirsty, use it with "at have" (to have): "Jeg har tørst" (I am thirsty), literally "I have thirst".

at udarbejde.explanation: "At udarbejde" means "to prepare", as in drawing up a document such as a report or a contract. It is built from "ud" (out) and "at arbejde" (to work). For everyday things like food, use "at lave" (to make): "Jeg laver mad" (I am making food).

at udbetale.explanation: "At udbetale" means "to pay out". To say a salary is paid: "Lønnen bliver udbetalt den første" (The salary is paid out on the first). The opposite is "at indbetale" (to pay in): "Jeg indbetaler penge på kontoen" (I pay money into the account).

at udbrede.explanation: "At udbrede" means "to spread", as in making an idea or news reach more people. For butter, use "at smøre" (to spread): "Jeg smører brødet" (I spread butter on the bread).

at udbygge.explanation: "At udbygge" means "to expand". It is built from "ud" (out) and "at bygge" (to build). To say a city adds to its roads: "De udbygger vejnettet" (They are expanding the road network).

at uddanne.explanation: "At uddanne" means "to educate", as in training someone for a profession. To say who does the training: "Hospitalet uddanner sygeplejersker" (The hospital trains nurses). To say you train yourself, add "sig" (yourself): "Jeg uddanner mig til lærer" (I am training to be a teacher).

at uddele.explanation: "At uddele" means "to hand out". To say someone gives things to a group: "Læreren uddeler opgaver" (The teacher hands out assignments). To say a prize is awarded, use "at tildele" (to award): "Hun blev tildelt prisen" (She was awarded the prize).

at udelade.explanation: "At udelade" means "to leave out". It is built from "ud" (out) and "at lade" (to let). To say you skip an ingredient: "Jeg udelader sukker i kaffen" (I leave sugar out of my coffee).

at udfase.explanation: "At udfase" means "to phase out". It is built from "ud" (out) and "en fase" (a phase). The opposite is "at indfase" (to phase in): "Kommunen indfaser en ny ordning" (The municipality is phasing in a new scheme).

at udfordre.explanation: "At udfordre" means "to challenge". To challenge someone to a contest, add "til" (to): "Jeg udfordrer dig til et løb" (I challenge you to a race).

at udforme.explanation: "At udforme" means "to design". It is built from "ud" (out) and "en form" (a shape). To say you design a plan: "Vi udformer en plan" (We are designing a plan).

at udforske.explanation: "At udforske" means "to explore". It is built from "ud" (out) and "at forske" (to research). To say you explore a city: "Vi udforsker byen til fods" (We explore the city on foot).

at udfylde.explanation: "At udfylde" means "to fill in". To say you complete a form: "Hun udfylder ansøgningen" (She fills in the application). To fill a glass, use "at fylde" (to fill): "Jeg fylder glasset" (I fill the glass).

at udføre.explanation: "At udføre" means "to carry out". To say someone does a job: "Han udfører arbejdet" (He carries out the work). To say you run a test: "Vi udfører en test" (We are running a test).

at udgive.explanation: "At udgive" means "to publish". To say someone pretends to be someone else, add "sig for" (oneself as): "Han udgav sig for en læge" (He posed as a doctor).

at udgrave.explanation: "At udgrave" means "to excavate". It is built from "ud" (out) and "at grave" (to dig). To say a team digs up old remains: "De udgraver en gammel gravplads" (They are excavating an old burial site).

at udgå.explanation: "At udgå" means "to be dropped". To say a product is taken out of a range: "Mælken udgår af sortimentet" (The milk is dropped from the range). To name the source something originates from, add "fra" (from): "Forslaget udgår fra ministeriet" (The proposal originates with the ministry).

at udgøre.explanation: "At udgøre" means "to constitute". To say what share something makes up: "Kvinder udgør halvdelen af klassen" (Women make up half of the class). To say something is dangerous, use it with "fare" (danger): "Det udgør en fare" (It poses a danger).

at udløbe.explanation: "At udløbe" means "to expire". It is built from "ud" (out) and "at løbe" (to run), so a time limit runs out. To ask when a document stops being valid: "Hvornår udløber dit pas?" (When does your passport expire?)

at udløse.explanation: "At udløse" means "to trigger". To say something sets off an alarm: "Røgen udløste alarmen" (The smoke set off the alarm). Do not mix it up with "at udløbe" (to expire): "Mit pas udløber i maj" (My passport expires in May).

at udmærke sig.explanation: "At udmærke sig" means "to excel". To name the quality you stand out for, add "ved" (for): "Hun udmærker sig ved sin flid" (She stands out for her hard work).

at udnytte.explanation: "At udnytte" means "to make use of". To say you make the most of your time: "at udnytte tiden" (to make the most of the time). About a person, it turns negative: "Han udnytter sine kolleger" (He takes advantage of his colleagues).

at udnævne.explanation: "At udnævne" means "to appoint". To name the position, add "til" (as): "udnævne nogen til dommer" (appoint someone as a judge).

at udrette.explanation: "At udrette" means "to accomplish". To say you cannot get anything done: "Jeg kan ikke udrette noget" (I cannot accomplish anything). To ask what can be done about a problem: "Hvad kan vi udrette?" (What can we do about it?)

at udrydde.explanation: "At udrydde" means "to eradicate". It is built from "ud" (out) and "at rydde" (to clear).

at udsende.explanation: "At udsende" means "to broadcast". It is built from "ud" (out) and "at sende" (to send). To say something gives off light: "Solen udsender lys og varme" (The sun gives off light and heat).

at udskifte.explanation: "At udskifte" means "to replace". To say you put a new part in place of an old one: "Jeg udskifter pæren" (I am replacing the light bulb).

at udslette.explanation: "At udslette" means "to wipe out". It is built from "ud" (out) and "at slette" (to erase).

at udstede.explanation: "At udstede" means "to issue". To say a bank gives out a card: "Banken udsteder et kort" (The bank issues a card). For a book or a magazine, use "at udgive" (to publish): "Forlaget udgiver bogen" (The publisher publishes the book).

at udstille.explanation: "At udstille" means "to exhibit". To say art is put on display: "Galleriet udstiller billeder" (The gallery exhibits pictures). To say someone is shown up in public, use it for a person: "Aviserne udstillede ham som løgner" (The papers exposed him as a liar).

at udsætte.explanation: "At udsætte" means "to postpone". To say a decision is put off: "Beslutningen er udsat til næste uge" (The decision is postponed until next week). To say you expose yourself to something unpleasant, add "sig for" (yourself to): "at udsætte sig for fare" (to expose yourself to danger).

at udtale.explanation: "At udtale" means "to pronounce". The noun is "en udtale" (a pronunciation). To compliment someone's speech: "Din udtale er god" (Your pronunciation is good).

at udtrykke.explanation: "At udtrykke" means "to express". To say someone voices an opinion: "Han udtrykker sin mening" (He expresses his opinion). To say how someone speaks, add "sig" (oneself): "Hun udtrykker sig klart" (She expresses herself clearly).

at udveksle.explanation: "At udveksle" means "to exchange". To say people give each other greetings: "De udvekslede hilsner" (They exchanged greetings). To swap an item for another, use "at bytte" (to swap): "Jeg bytter trøjen" (I am swapping the sweater).

at udvide.explanation: "At udvide" means "to expand". To say a company grows its premises: "Firmaet udvider med et nyt kontor" (The company is expanding with a new office). For something that grows by itself, use "at vokse" (to grow): "Byen vokser" (The town grows).

at udvikle.explanation: "At udvikle" means "to develop". To say someone grows and changes, add "sig" (oneself): "Børn udvikler sig hurtigt" (Children develop quickly).

at udvikle sig.explanation: "At udvikle sig" means "to develop". To say someone improves step by step: "Hun udvikler sig som musiker" (She is developing as a musician). The "sig" (oneself) is needed for this meaning. To say someone builds something, use "at udvikle" without "sig": "at udvikle en app" (to develop an app).

at udvælge.explanation: "At udvælge" means "to select". To say you pick a few from many: "Hun udvælger de bedste billeder" (She selects the best photos). For a quick choice, use "at vælge" (to choose): "Jeg vælger kaffe" (I choose coffee).

at underholde.explanation: "At underholde" means "to entertain". With "sig" (oneself), it means to chat: "De underholdt sig hele aftenen" (They chatted all evening).

at underkaste sig.explanation: "At underkaste sig" means "to submit to". To say people accept a rule, name it after the verb: "De måtte underkaste sig reglerne" (They had to submit to the rules). It is built from "under" (under) and "at kaste" (to throw).

at underminere.explanation: "At underminere" means "to undermine". To say someone weakens authority: "Han underminerer lærerens autoritet" (He undermines the teacher's authority).

at underrette.explanation: "At underrette" means "to notify". To say you tell the police about an accident: "Jeg underretter politiet om uheldet" (I notify the police about the accident).
